title: Scrum Ceremonies Done Right
description: Scrum’s four ceremonies are the workflow’s heartbeat, and each has a failure mode the discipline prevents. Sprint planning (2–4 hours): the team — not the manager — commits to the sprint goal and backlog, with capacity honestly accounted; the failure is the dictated plan nobody believes. The daily Scrum (15 minutes): each member states progress, plan, and blockers — a synchronization, not a status report to a boss; the failure is the 45-minute problem-solving session. The sprint review: working software demoed to stakeholders, feedback captured as backlog input; the failure is the slide deck review with nothing running. The retrospective: the team inspects its process and commits to one improvement; the failure is the complaint session with no action. The product backlog refinement (ongoing): the product owner and team clarify upcoming work so planning starts from understanding. The meta-discipline: timeboxes are sacred — ceremonies that expand fill the calendar and kill the maker time the sprints need.
key_points: Planning: team commits; capacity honestly counted
Daily: synchronization, not status reporting
Review: working software, not slides
Retrospective: one committed improvement
core_principles: Inspect and adapt the process itself
how_it_works: Run the four ceremonies plus refinement on fixed cadence; protect timeboxes; act on retrospective commitments.
best_fit: Product teams shipping incrementally.

title: Kanban Systems
description: Kanban manages flow rather than iterations: work items move across a board (to do, doing, done) with work-in-progress limits that expose bottlenecks. The core practices: visualize the workflow, limit WIP (the discipline that makes everything else work — unfinished work is inventory, and inventory hides problems), manage flow (measure lead time and throughput, not just busyness), make policies explicit (definition of done per column), and improve collaboratively. The WIP limit is the genius: when the “doing” column fills, the team must finish work before starting more — which surfaces the blocked item, the overloaded specialist, the unclear requirement. Cumulative flow diagrams show the system’s health at a glance: widening bands mean growing WIP and slowing delivery. Kanban fits continuous-flow work — support teams, ops, marketing — where sprints would be artificial. The failure mode is board theater: a pretty board with no WIP limits, which is just a to-do list with extra steps.
key_points: Visualize flow; limit WIP; measure lead time
WIP limits expose bottlenecks — finish before starting
Cumulative flow diagrams show system health
Fits continuous flow: support, ops, marketing
how_it_works: Map the workflow to columns, set WIP limits, pull work through, measure flow, improve the bottlenecks.
best_fit: Continuous-flow teams: support, ops, marketing.

title: SAFe: Scaled Agile Framework
description: SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework, Dean Leffingwell) scales Agile to enterprises: Agile Release Trains (ARTs) of 50–125 people plan together in PI (Program Increment) planning — two days, all teams, every 8–12 weeks — aligning on objectives and dependencies. The roles scale: Release Train Engineer (the ART’s Scrum master), Product Management (the train’s product owner), System Architect. The practices: the program kanban for features, the architectural runway (just-enough forward architecture), and inspect-and-adapt workshops per PI. SAFe’s power is coordination at scale — hundreds of engineers planning together beats hundreds planning separately. The criticism is weight: SAFe’s full configuration has dozens of roles and artifacts, and critics call it “waterfall in agile clothing” when implemented as process compliance. The honest assessment: SAFe works where enterprises need its coordination and implement its spirit (inspect-and-adapt, working software); where they implement only its ceremonies, it is expensive theater. Lighter alternatives (LeSS, Nexus, Spotify-style) suit smaller scales.
key_points: ARTs of 50–125 plan together in PI planning
Roles: RTE, Product Management, System Architect
Power: coordination at enterprise scale
Risk: process compliance without agility
core_principles: Align the train, empower the teams
how_it_works: Form ARTs, run PI planning quarterly, execute iterations, demo system-wide, inspect-and-adapt per PI.
best_fit: Enterprises coordinating 100+ engineers on shared products.

title: Lean Startup and Build-Measure-Learn
description: The Lean Startup (Eric Ries, 2011) brought lean thinking to new ventures: build-measure-learn loops that test business hypotheses with minimum viable products instead of building on untested assumptions. The MVP is the smallest thing that tests the hypothesis — a landing page testing demand, a concierge service testing the experience manually, a single-feature app testing the core interaction. Validated learning is the unit of progress: what did we learn, measured by actionable metrics (cohort retention, conversion) rather than vanity metrics (total signups). Pivot or persevere: the loop’s decision — change the strategy on validated evidence, or double down. Innovation accounting adapts the metrics to startups: baseline, tune the engine, pivot-or-persevere. The power is waste elimination at the strategy level — the biggest waste is building what nobody wants. The misapplication: “MVP” as an excuse for shoddy quality, or endless pivoting without conviction. Best fit: new products and ventures under uncertainty.
key_points: Build-measure-learn loops test hypotheses
MVP: smallest test of the riskiest assumption
Validated learning via actionable metrics
Pivot or persevere on evidence
how_it_works: State hypotheses, build the MVP, measure actionable metrics, learn, pivot or persevere, repeat.
best_fit: New products and ventures under uncertainty.

title: Value Stream Mapping
description: Value stream mapping makes the whole workflow visible — the prerequisite for improving it. The method: pick one product family, walk the actual flow (go to the gemba — the real place), and draw the current-state map: process boxes with cycle times, inventory triangles with wait times, information flows above, and the timeline at the bottom separating value-added time from total lead time. The ratio shocks first-timers: value-added time is typically 1–5% of lead time — the rest is waiting, the purest waste. The future-state map then designs the flow: continuous flow where possible, pull where not, one improvement at a time. The mapping workshop’s rules: cross-functional participants (the people who do the work), data over opinions (measure the waits), and the future state drawn the same day (momentum matters). The map’s power is shared sight — arguments about priorities end when everyone sees the same 95% waste. Re-map yearly; flows drift.
key_points: Walk the actual flow; draw current state with times
Value-added is typically 1–5% of lead time
Future state: continuous flow, pull, one improvement at a time
Shared sight ends priority arguments
core_principles: See the whole before improving the parts
how_it_works: Pick a product family, walk the gemba, map current state with times, design future state, implement stepwise, re-map yearly.
best_fit: Any repeatable workflow with handoffs.

title: Kaizen: Continuous Improvement Systems
description: Kaizen — continuous improvement by everyone, every day — is lean’s cultural engine, and it runs on systems, not slogans. The suggestion system: every employee can propose improvements, proposals get fast responses (the 24-hour acknowledgment rule), implemented ideas get recognized, and the best get shared across the company. Kaizen events (blitzes): week-long focused improvements on one process, with the team empowered to change it and the results measured. Daily kaizen: the team board where today’s small problems get today’s countermeasures — the 5-minute fixes that compound. Leadership’s role is gemba walks — going to the work, asking why, coaching the improvement — not approving from the office. The metrics: ideas per person per year (Toyota’s millions), implementation rate, and the savings/quality gains. The failure mode is the suggestion box — proposals into a void, no response, no implementation — which teaches employees that improvement is unwelcome. Kaizen lives on response speed.
key_points: Suggestion systems with 24-hour acknowledgment
Kaizen blitzes: week-long focused improvements
Daily kaizen: today’s problems, today’s countermeasures
Leadership does gemba walks, not office approvals
core_principles: Respond fast or kill the culture
how_it_works: Install suggestion flow, run blitzes quarterly, hold daily improvement huddles, leaders walk the gemba weekly.
best_fit: Operations with stable workforces and repeatable work.

title: DMAIC Project Workflow
description: DMAIC is Six Sigma’s project workflow — five phases that take a problem from charter to controlled improvement. Define: the project charter — problem statement, scope, goals, team, business case; SIPOC maps the process boundaries. Measure: baseline the current performance — data collection plans, measurement system analysis (is the data trustworthy?), process capability. Analyze: find root causes — hypothesis tests, regression, designed experiments separating the vital few causes from the trivial many. Improve: implement solutions — pilot first, verify with data, then full rollout. Control: lock in the gains — control plans, monitoring charts, response procedures, handoff to process owners. Tollgates between phases keep projects honest: no phase proceeds on hope. A DMAIC project runs 3–6 months with a trained belt leading; the financial tracking (verified savings) justifies the rigor. The discipline: data at every gate, or the project is opinion with a charter.
key_points: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control
Tollgates: no phase proceeds on hope
3–6 months per project with a trained belt
Verified savings justify the rigor
how_it_works: Charter, baseline, analyze statistically, pilot improvements, control with monitoring, hand off to owners.
best_fit: Complex quality problems with measurable impact.

title: Stage-Gate Product Development
description: Stage-Gate (Robert Cooper) structures product development as stages separated by gates: each stage does the work, each gate decides go/kill/hold/recycle on evidence. The classic five stages: scoping, business case, development, testing and validation, launch — with gates reviewing deliverables against must-meet and should-meet criteria. Gatekeepers are senior managers with the authority to kill — the gate’s power is the kill decision, because portfolios die from zombie projects that gates would not kill. The deliverables per stage are defined upfront: the business case gate needs market data and financials, not enthusiasm. Modern variants (Agile-Stage-Gate) blend iterative development inside stages with the gates’ portfolio discipline. The power: resource focus — killing weak projects early funds the strong ones. The risk: gate bureaucracy slowing fast markets, and gates as political theater. The discipline: criteria defined before the project, killers empowered, and post-launch reviews that score the gate decisions.
key_points: Stages do work; gates decide go/kill on evidence
Gate power is the kill decision
Criteria defined upfront, not improvised
Agile-Stage-Gate blends iteration with portfolio discipline
how_it_works: Define stages and gate criteria, execute stages, hold gates with empowered gatekeepers, review launches, score decisions.
best_fit: Physical products and regulated development.

title: The Weekly Execution Cadence (Level 10)
description: EOS’s Level 10 Meeting is the best-documented weekly execution cadence in small business: 90 minutes, same agenda, same time, starting on time. The agenda: 5 minutes segue (good news), 5 minutes scorecard review (every number on/off track — off-track numbers become issues), 5 minutes rock review (quarterly priorities on/off track), 5 minutes headlines (customer and employee news), 5 minutes to-do list review, 60 minutes IDS (identify, discuss, solve the top issues — prioritized, discussed to root cause, solved with an owner and deadline), 5 minutes conclude (recap to-dos, rate the meeting 1–10). The disciplines: the same time weekly (rhythm beats inspiration), starting on time (lateness disrespects the system), IDS on root causes (solving the same issue weekly means the root cause was missed), and the meeting rating (below 8 means fix the meeting). The power: a company that truly runs its Level 10 never lets issues fester past a week. The requirement: the leadership team’s full attendance and honesty.
key_points: 90 minutes, same agenda, same time weekly
IDS: identify, discuss, solve to root cause
Scorecard plus rocks plus headlines in 25 minutes
Rate the meeting; below 8 means fix it
core_principles: Issues never fester past a week
how_it_works: Run the fixed agenda weekly with full leadership attendance; IDS the top issues; track to-dos; rate and improve.
best_fit: Leadership teams running EOS or similar systems.

title: Quarterly Planning Rhythms
description: Quarterly planning translates annual strategy into 90-day execution, and the rhythm’s design decides whether quarters compound or just pass. The session (1–2 days offsite): review last quarter (score the rocks/OKRs honestly — the 70% conversation), assess the landscape (market, competition, internal capacity), set the quarterly priorities (3–7 rocks, each with a single owner and a done-definition), align the scorecard (are we measuring what matters now?), and surface the quarter’s key issues. The disciplines: fewer priorities than feel comfortable (focus is saying no), owners not committees, done-definitions not activity descriptions, and the plan published to the company within 48 hours. The weekly cadence then executes the quarterly plan; the quarterly review then scores it — the loop closes. The failure modes: the 20-priority quarter (no priorities), the plan nobody reads (no publication), and the quarter that never gets reviewed (no learning). Ninety days is the human planning horizon — long enough to matter, short enough to stay real.
key_points: 1–2 day offsite: review, assess, prioritize, align
3–7 priorities with owners and done-definitions
Publish within 48 hours; review honestly next quarter
90 days: long enough to matter, short enough to be real
how_it_works: Offsite quarterly, set few owned priorities, publish fast, execute weekly, score honestly, learn, repeat.
best_fit: Any company running a deliberate OS.

title: Hoshin Kanri: Policy Deployment
description: Hoshin kanri — policy deployment, Toyota’s strategy-execution system — aligns the entire company behind a few breakthrough objectives through catchball: the iterative back-and-forth where each level proposes how it will contribute to the objectives above, negotiated until alignment is real. The annual cycle: top leadership sets 3–5 hoshins (breakthrough objectives — not incremental targets), each level deploys them via catchball into its own objectives and plans, execution runs with monthly reviews, and the year ends with reflection (hansei) feeding next year’s hoshins. The X-matrix (a one-page diagram linking objectives, strategies, metrics, and owners) makes the deployment visible. The power: true alignment — every level’s plan demonstrably serves the breakthrough objectives, unlike cascading goals that dilute downward. The discipline: few hoshins (the system cannot deploy ten), genuine catchball (not dictated cascades), and the reflection step (hansei prevents repeating failures). Best fit: manufacturing and large operations needing true strategic alignment.
key_points: Catchball: iterative negotiation aligns every level
3–5 breakthrough hoshins yearly, not incremental targets
X-matrix makes deployment visible
Hansei reflection feeds next year
how_it_works: Set hoshins, catchball down the levels, execute with monthly review, reflect yearly, feed forward.
best_fit: Manufacturing and large operations.

title: Continuous Delivery and DevOps Flow
description: Continuous delivery brings manufacturing flow thinking to software: every commit is a candidate for production, and the deployment pipeline (build, test, stage, deploy) makes releases routine rather than events. The practices: trunk-based development (short-lived branches, integrated daily), comprehensive test automation (the pipeline’s quality gate), deployment automation (one-button or zero-button releases), feature flags (decoupling deployment from release), and monitoring as a first-class concern (you build it, you run it). The metrics are DORA’s four: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore — elite performers deploy on demand with hour-scale lead times. The cultural shift is DevOps proper: developers own production outcomes, operations engineers build platforms, and blameless postmortems turn incidents into learning. The power: speed with safety — small batches fail small and recover fast. The requirement: test automation investment and the cultural shift; the pipeline without the culture is just faster chaos.
key_points: Every commit production-ready; releases routine
DORA metrics: frequency, lead time, failure rate, restore time
Feature flags decouple deploy from release
Blameless postmortems turn incidents into learning
core_principles: You build it, you run it
how_it_works: Build the pipeline, automate tests, flag features, deploy small, monitor everything, postmortem blamelessly.
watch_outs: Pipeline without culture is faster chaos
best_fit: Software organizations shipping frequently.

title: Blameless Postmortems
description: Blameless postmortems turn incidents into organizational learning instead of punishment — the practice that separates learning cultures from fear cultures. The format: timeline reconstruction (what happened, minute by minute, from logs and testimony), impact assessment, root-cause analysis via “five whys” (asking why repeatedly until reaching systemic causes, never stopping at human error), and action items with owners and deadlines. The blameless rule is structural: the postmortem asks what allowed the mistake, not who made it — because punishment drives incidents underground while systems thinking prevents recurrence. The disciplines: hold the postmortem within days (memory fades), include everyone involved (the full picture needs all views), publish the writeup (the organization learns, not just the team), and track action items to completion (unfinished actions teach that postmortems are theater). Google’s SRE book made the practice famous; aviation’s accident investigation is its ancestor. The test: do engineers report near-misses voluntarily? If yes, the culture is blameless; if no, incidents are being hidden.
key_points: Timeline, impact, five-whys root cause, owned actions
Blameless: what allowed it, never who did it
Publish writeups; track actions to completion
Near-miss reporting is the culture test
core_principles: Systems fail; people err within systems
how_it_works: Hold within days, reconstruct fully, five-whys to systemic causes, assign owned actions, publish, track.
best_fit: Any operations with incidents worth learning from.

title: The 5S Workplace System
description: 5S (sort, set in order, shine, standardize, sustain) is lean’s workplace organization system — deceptively simple, transformative in practice. Sort (seiri): remove everything not needed for the work — the red-tag event where questionable items get tagged and removed. Set in order (seiton): a place for everything, everything in its place — shadow boards, labeled locations, the 30-second retrieval test (any tool found in 30 seconds). Shine (seiso): clean to inspect — cleaning reveals leaks, wear, and abnormalities. Standardize (seiketsu): make the first three Ss the normal way — checklists, photos of the correct state, audits. Sustain (shitsuke): the discipline — regular audits, management gemba walks, making 5S part of the job not an extra. The power: an organized workplace exposes problems (the oil leak visible on the clean floor) and saves the compounded minutes of searching. The failure: the “cleaning campaign” without sustain — entropy returns within weeks. 5S is the foundation other lean tools build on.
key_points: Sort, set in order, shine, standardize, sustain
30-second retrieval test for every tool
Clean to inspect: shine reveals abnormalities
Sustain via audits and gemba walks
how_it_works: Red-tag sort, organize with shadow boards, clean-inspect, photograph standards, audit regularly.
best_fit: Any physical workplace; adaptable to digital.

title: Gemba Walks
description: The gemba walk — going to the real place where work happens — is lean leadership’s core discipline: managers learn by observing reality instead of managing by report. The practice: leaders walk the floor (or the virtual equivalent) regularly, observe the work as it actually happens, ask why (respectfully, curiously — the walk is not an inspection), and coach problem-solving rather than solving problems for people. The three questions: what is the standard? What is the actual? What is the gap — and what will you try? The disciplines: go often enough to see normal (not just crises), stay long enough to observe (not drive-bys), follow up on what you heard (the walk that changes nothing teaches cynicism), and never use observations punitively (the walk is for learning). The power: leaders who know the real work make real decisions; the gemba walk is the antidote to conference-room management. The virtual gemba: screen-shares, ticket queues, and dashboards walked with the same curiosity.
key_points: Go to the real place; observe reality
Ask why respectfully — the walk is not an inspection
Coach problem-solving; do not solve for people
Follow up or teach cynicism
how_it_works: Schedule walks, observe the actual work, ask the three questions, coach, follow up, repeat.
best_fit: Leaders at every level in any operation.

title: Standard Work and SOP Discipline
description: Standard work — the documented current best way to do a task — is the baseline that makes improvement possible: without a standard, there is no “better,” only “different.” The standard work sheet: the task’s steps in sequence, key points per step (quality and safety criticals), time per step, and the reason behind non-obvious steps (so workers improve the method, not just follow it). The disciplines: standards written by the people who do the work (with supervision), trained via job instruction (show, explain, watch, verify — not “read this”), followed until improved (deviation requires proposing the improvement), and improved through kaizen (the standard is always the current best, never the permanent way). The paradox newcomers miss: standardization enables creativity — the stable baseline frees attention for improvement instead of reinvention. The failure: standards written by offices, ignored on floors — the binder that nobody opens. Living standards live where the work happens.
key_points: Documented current best way — the baseline for improvement
Written by doers; trained by demonstration
Followed until improved via kaizen
Standardization enables creativity
how_it_works: Document with doers, train by job instruction, follow, improve through kaizen, update the standard.
best_fit: Repeatable work of any kind.

title: Andon and Stop-the-Line Culture
description: Andon — Toyota’s cord that any worker pulls to stop the line for a defect — embodies the quality culture most companies claim and few practice: stopping production is cheaper than shipping defects. The system: the cord (or button, or signal) summons help immediately; the team swarms the problem at the spot; if unresolved in the takt time, the line stops; the defect’s root cause gets countermeasured before restart. The cultural prerequisites: workers must be safe pulling the cord (no punishment for stops — the metric is problems surfaced, not uptime protected), leaders must respond to andons as the priority (the cord that summons nobody teaches helplessness), and the organization must prefer the short stop to the long defect avalanche. The software translation: anyone can freeze a deploy, roll back a release, or page the team — with the same protections. The economics: a minute stopped beats a thousand defects shipped. The test: when did someone last stop your line? If never, the cord is decoration.
key_points: Any worker stops the line for a defect
Swarm the problem; countermeasure before restart
Safety to pull: metric is problems surfaced
A minute stopped beats a thousand defects shipped
core_principles: Stop and fix beats ship and sort
how_it_works: Install the signal, train the response, protect pullers, swarm problems, countermeasure roots, track stops as health.
best_fit: Production and delivery operations of any kind.

title: Poka-Yoke: Mistake-Proofing
description: Poka-yoke — mistake-proofing, Shigeo Shingo’s contribution to Toyota — designs errors out of processes instead of inspecting them out. The three levels: prevention (the error cannot occur — the asymmetrical connector that fits only one way), detection (the error is caught immediately — the sensor that stops the machine when the part is missing), and the warning (the error is flagged — the least preferred, still better than escape). The methods: physical guides and fixtures, checklists with forced sequence, sensors and interlocks, and software validation (the form that will not submit with a bad date). The economics: mistake-proofing costs once and prevents forever, while inspection costs every unit and catches imperfectly. The design discipline: study where errors actually occur (the defect data), attack the frequent and the severe, and prefer prevention over detection over warning. Software’s poka-yoke: types that make illegal states unrepresentable, defaults that are safe, confirmations for destructive actions. The principle: respect human fallibility by designing for it.
key_points: Prevention beats detection beats warning
Design errors out; do not inspect them out
Costs once, prevents forever
Study defect data; attack frequent and severe
core_principles: Design for the error, not against the human
how_it_works: Study error data, design prevention/detection per error, implement, verify error rates drop, standardize.
best_fit: Any process with repeatable error modes.

title: Total Productive Maintenance (TPM)
description: Total Productive Maintenance makes equipment reliability everyone’s job — operators, not just technicians, own their machines’ basic care. The eight pillars: autonomous maintenance (operators clean, lubricate, inspect, and tighten daily — the abnormalities they find are the early warnings), planned maintenance (scheduled by condition and time), quality maintenance (defect prevention at the source), focused improvement (kaizen on the chronic losses), early equipment management (reliability designed into new purchases), training, safety/health/environment, and TPM in administration. The metric is OEE — overall equipment effectiveness (availability × performance × quality) — with world-class at 85%. The cultural shift: operators as the equipment’s first line of defense, technicians as the specialists for the hard problems, and the war on the six big losses (breakdowns, setups, idling, reduced speed, defects, startup losses). The economics: unplanned downtime costs 5–10x planned maintenance. TPM’s lesson: reliability is built daily by everyone, not repaired occasionally by specialists.
key_points: Operators own daily care: clean, lubricate, inspect
OEE: availability x performance x quality; 85% world-class
War on the six big losses
Unplanned downtime costs 5–10x planned maintenance
how_it_works: Train operators in autonomous care, schedule planned maintenance, track OEE, kaizen the losses, design reliability into purchases.
best_fit: Equipment-intensive operations.

title: The Daily Huddle
description: The daily huddle — 5–15 minutes, standing, same time — is the smallest coordination ritual with the largest ROI in company workflows. The format: each person states their top priority today, any blocker, and any help needed — 60 seconds each, no problem-solving (blockers get owners and offline time). Variations: the sales huddle (numbers and stuck deals), the production huddle (yesterday’s output, today’s plan, andon issues), the leadership huddle (cross-functional blockers and priorities). The disciplines: same time daily (rhythm over convenience), standing (brevity enforced physically), start on time even if incomplete (the late learn), and the parking lot for everything else. The power: 24-hour issue latency — nothing waits past tomorrow morning — and the ambient awareness that prevents duplicate work and surprise dependencies. The failure: the huddle that becomes a meeting (problem-solving in the circle), or the huddle nobody misses because nothing happens there. Fifteen minutes that run the day.
key_points: 5–15 min standing; priority, blocker, help needed
No problem-solving in the circle — owners plus offline
24-hour issue latency; ambient awareness
Start on time even if incomplete
how_it_works: Set the time, run the 60-second format standing, assign blocker owners, park the rest, protect the ritual.
best_fit: Any team with daily coordination needs.

title: A3 Problem Solving
description: The A3 — Toyota’s one-page (A3 paper size) problem-solving report — forces rigorous thinking into a single sheet: no hiding behind decks. The left side: background, current condition (with data and a diagram), goals/targets. The right side: root-cause analysis (five whys, fishbone), countermeasures, implementation plan, and follow-up (did it work?). The disciplines: the author owns the investigation (goes to the gemba, gathers facts), the mentor reviews by questioning (never rewriting — the thinking must be the author’s), and the A3 is a conversation document, not a submission — it gets discussed, marked up, and revised. The power: concision forces clarity — the problem that cannot fit one page is not understood yet. Nemawashi (consensus-building before the decision) happens through the A3’s circulation. The failure: A3 as paperwork — filled after the decision to justify it. The test: does the A3 change minds? If yes, it is thinking; if no, it is theater.
key_points: One page: background to follow-up
Author investigates; mentor questions, never rewrites
Concision forces clarity
A conversation document, not a submission
core_principles: Fit the thinking on one page
how_it_works: Author investigates at the gemba, drafts the A3, circulates for nemawashi, discusses with mentor, implements, follows up.
best_fit: Organizations building problem-solving capability.

title: Obeya: The Big Room
description: Obeya — Japanese for “big room” — co-locates a project’s leadership in one visual workspace where the plan, status, and problems live on the walls. Toyota’s product development obeya: the chief engineer’s room with the program’s targets, timelines, design status, and issues displayed — leaders meet there, decide there, the walls holding the shared truth. The disciplines: the room reflects reality (updated, honest — the wall that lies is worse than no wall), the right people meet there regularly (decision-makers, not representatives’ representatives), and problems come to the room (andon for projects). The digital obeya translates the practice: the dashboard, the virtual war room, the always-current program page — with the same disciplines (honest, current, decision-makers present). The power: shared visual truth collapses alignment time — the meeting starts from the walls, not from competing slide decks. The failure: the showroom obeya — beautiful walls, real work elsewhere.
key_points: Project leadership co-located in one visual workspace
Walls hold the shared truth: targets, status, issues
Decide in the room; problems come to the room
Digital obeya needs the same disciplines
how_it_works: Stand up the room (physical or digital), populate honestly, meet there with deciders, keep current, decide there.
best_fit: Complex programs needing tight coordination.

title: Workflow Metrics That Matter
description: Workflow metrics should guide improvement, not feed vanity — the useful set is small. Flow metrics: lead time (idea to delivery — the customer’s experience of your speed), cycle time (start to finish of active work), throughput (items completed per period), and WIP (the inventory hiding your problems). Quality metrics: defect rate, escaped defects, rework percentage — the cost of poor flow. Predictability metrics: due-date performance, estimation accuracy — the trust metrics. Improvement metrics: kaizen ideas implemented, action-item completion — the system improving itself. The disciplines: measure the system, not individuals (individual metrics breed gaming and fear); trend over snapshot (direction matters more than the number); and review metrics in the improvement forum, not the blame forum. Goodhart’s law governs all of it: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure — rotate and triangulate. The test: do the metrics change behavior for the better? If yes, keep them; if no, they are wallpaper.
key_points: Flow: lead time, cycle time, throughput, WIP
Quality: defects, escapes, rework
Measure systems, not individuals
Goodhart’s law: rotate and triangulate
how_it_works: Pick the small useful set, instrument honestly, review in improvement forums, act on trends, rotate targets.
best_fit: Any workflow being deliberately improved.

title: Choosing and Combining Workflows
description: No single workflow fits a whole company — the art is choosing per unit and combining coherently. The selection logic: product development under uncertainty gets Agile/Lean Startup (empirical, iterative); repeatable operations get Lean/Six Sigma (flow, variation reduction); creative work gets Kanban plus WIP limits (flow without sprint artificiality); enterprise coordination gets scaled patterns (SAFe, obeya) where scale demands. The combination disciplines: name the workflow per unit explicitly (the “we’re agile” vagueness helps nobody), design the handoffs between workflows (dev’s Scrum to ops’ Kanban needs an interface), keep the company cadence common (quarterly planning, weekly execution — the shared heartbeat across different workflows), and let units evolve their workflows with coaching. The failure: the mandated single workflow (Scrum for the legal team) or the undeclared mix (every team different, nobody interoperable). The principle: workflows serve the work — fit the method to the work’s nature, and keep the company’s heartbeat shared.
key_points: Choose per unit: match method to work nature
Design handoffs between different workflows
Keep company cadence common across units
Workflows serve the work, not vice versa
how_it_works: Map units’ work natures, choose workflows explicitly, design interfaces, hold common cadence, coach evolution.
best_fit: Multi-unit companies with varied work.
